profile.research_note:
Current operator of this cable landing station following the 2020 T-Mobile merger and 2023-2024 Cogent wireline sale is unresolved; retained under Sprint per no-reassignment-without-confirmation policy.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Manasquan Cable Landing Station in Manasquan, New Jersey, terminating the TAT-14 transatlantic fiber optic cable system, a consortium cable that entered service in 2001 connecting the United States to the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Denmark, and the Netherlands. Sprint Corporation, a Kansas based wireless and wireline carrier, was one of the original TAT-14 consortium members alongside carriers including AT&T, Verizon, France Telecom, and Deutsche Telekom, each historically responsible for landing and operating a segment of the shared cable system. Sprint merged into T-Mobile US on April 1, 2020. Following that merger, T-Mobile sold the bulk of its legacy wireline business, including more than thirty former Sprint network switch sites converted to colocation space, to Cogent Communications in a deal announced May 2023 and closed 2024, structured as a one dollar sale with revenue sharing terms. No source found in this research confirms whether this Manasquan landing station specifically was included in that Cogent transaction, since cable landing stations tied to multi carrier consortium cables are often governed separately from ordinary switch and colocation real estate; current operational control of this facility is not published and is treated as unresolved. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project and is reused here for the facility record.

reading.body:
This facility is a cable landing station, not a data center campus. It terminates the TAT-14 transatlantic fiber optic cable system, which has connected the United States to the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Denmark, and the Netherlands since 2001. The published specifications provide no information about the building's power capacity, cooling capability, or IT load. Current operational control of the facility is unresolved following T-Mobile's 2020 acquisition of Sprint and subsequent 2023-2024 sale of legacy wireline assets to Cogent Communications, with no published source confirming whether this landing station was included in that transaction.

Cable landing stations are critical infrastructure for transatlantic data movement but are functionally distinct from the colocation and purpose-built data center campuses that host AI training clusters. They concentrate bandwidth termination rather than compute density. Without published power specifications, this site cannot be ranked alongside the five New Jersey facilities with published megawatt figures, which together represent 111.3 MW of stated capacity across 48 mapped facilities in the state.

For readers assessing whether this location matters to AI scaling, the answer depends on connectivity rather than local compute. If you are evaluating where training clusters can be sited to reach international markets with low latency, a functional TAT-14 landing station matters. If you are counting US data center capacity or power availability for AI workloads, this facility contributes neither a published specification nor confirmed operational status.
